title: Find the Maximum Length of Valid Subsequence I
statement:
A **subsequence** of the integer array `nums` is what remains after deleting zero or more of its elements, with the rest kept in their original order. A subsequence `sub` of length `x` is **valid** when the sums of its neighbouring elements, `sub[0] + sub[1]`, `sub[1] + sub[2]`, ..., `sub[x - 2] + sub[x - 1]`, all have the same parity: every one of them is even, or every one of them is odd.

Return the greatest length that a valid subsequence of `nums` can have.
notes:
## Intuition

A sum of two integers is even exactly when both have the same parity, and odd exactly when their parities differ. So a valid subsequence has one of only three shapes: every element even, every element odd (all sums even), or parities that alternate (all sums odd). The first two are easy: take every even number, or every odd number.

For the alternating shape, think of `nums` as blocks of neighbouring numbers with equal parity. An alternating subsequence can use at most one number from each block, and greedily taking a number whenever its parity differs from the last one taken uses exactly one per block. A brute force could try all 2^n subsequences instead, or run an O(n²) dynamic program over pairs.

## Approach

1. Count the even numbers in `evens` and the odd ones in `odds`.
2. Build the alternating subsequence greedily: `alternating` is its length and `lastParity` the parity of the last number it took (`-1` before the first, so the first number is always taken).
3. For each `num`, compute `parity = num % 2` and add it to its count. When `parity` differs from `lastParity`, take the number: increase `alternating` and update `lastParity`.
4. Return the largest of `evens`, `odds` and `alternating`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]` has parities 1, 0, 1, 0. Each number differs in parity from the one before, so the greedy subsequence takes all four: `alternating = 4`. Meanwhile `evens = 2` (2 and 4) and `odds = 2` (1 and 3). The answer is `max(2, 2, 4) = 4`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass over `nums`.
- Space: O(1): three counters and one remembered parity.

## Pitfalls

- Forgetting the all-sums-even shape: `[1, 3]` has an even sum and is valid with length 2.
- Requiring the alternation to start with an odd (or an even) number: the greedy pass starts from the first number, whatever its parity.
- Treating the subsequence as a contiguous subarray: elements may be skipped.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `evens`, `odds` | how many even and odd numbers `nums` holds |
| `alternating` | length of the greedy subsequence with alternating parities |
| `lastParity` | parity of the last number that subsequence took (`-1` before any) |
| `num`, `parity` | the current number and its remainder modulo 2 |
